reference.source: Greenspan, Orthopedic Imaging: A Practical Approach
clinicalPearls: A focus of compact cortical bone within the cancellous medullary bone, most often an incidental finding in the pelvis, proximal femur and other long bones.
The hallmark radiographic feature is a homogeneously dense sclerotic focus with radiating spiculated thorny or brush-border margins that blend into the surrounding trabeculae.
The lesion is typically asymptomatic and stable, although slow growth can occur over years.

Bone scintigraphy usually shows little or no increased uptake, which helps distinguish it from osteoblastic metastasis that is typically intensely avid, though large or growing islands may show mild uptake.
CT attenuation is very high, often in the range of dense cortical bone, which helps separate it from lower-attenuation sclerotic metastases.

Multiple bone islands define osteopoikilosis, an autosomal dominant condition caused by LEMD3 mutations that may occur with the skin lesions of Buschke-Ollendorff syndrome (dermatofibrosis lenticularis disseminata).
A lesion larger than about 2 cm is termed a giant bone island; slow growth is acceptable but marked or rapid enlargement warrants scrutiny.
No treatment is required; the key clinical value is confident recognition to avoid unnecessary biopsy or oncological work-up.
reference.pathophysiology: A bone island, or enostosis, is a benign developmental hamartomatous focus of mature compact (lamellar) bone situated within the spongiosa. It is thought to result from a localised failure of osteoclastic resorption during endochondral ossification and remodelling, leaving an island of dense cortical-type bone that maintains continuity with the surrounding trabeculae through its characteristic radiating bony spicules. Histologically it consists of normal lamellar bone with Haversian systems, and it possesses no malignant potential. When multiple and symmetrically distributed, particularly in a periarticular distribution, the lesions represent osteopoikilosis, linked to loss-of-function mutations in the LEMD3 gene.
additionalDifferentials: Osteoblastic metastasis (notably prostate and breast carcinoma)
Healed or sclerotic phase of a prior benign lesion
additionalInvestigations: Plain radiographs demonstrating a dense focus with radiating spiculated margins
CT to document very high attenuation approaching that of cortical bone
Bone scintigraphy to assess for the intense uptake that would favour metastasis
Comparison with prior imaging to confirm stability or characterise growth
MRI in selected uncertain cases, where the lesion is low signal on all sequences
Correlation with tumour markers and primary tumour history when metastasis is a concern
redFlags: Significant interval growth, particularly more than about 1 cm per year
Associated lucency, cortical destruction or a soft-tissue mass
Intense uptake on bone scintigraphy with a known primary malignancy or rising tumour markers
New localised pain attributable to the lesion
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent; the bone island is entirely benign with no malignant potential and requires only recognition rather than treatment.
pitfalls: Misinterpreting a bone island as an osteoblastic metastasis, or dismissing a true metastasis as a bone island
Proceeding to unnecessary biopsy of a radiographically classic lesion
Failing to act on documented marked interval growth
Overlooking the pattern of osteopoikilosis and its familial and cutaneous associations

management: No treatment is required, as the lesion is entirely benign with no malignant potential and management is recognition and reassurance
Confirm the diagnosis radiologically by the dense sclerotic focus with radiating spiculated margins and very high CT attenuation approaching cortical bone
Use bone scintigraphy and comparison with prior imaging to distinguish it from osteoblastic metastasis, avoiding unnecessary biopsy
Interval follow-up imaging only where the lesion is large, growing or diagnostically uncertain, to document stability
When multiple islands indicate osteopoikilosis, consider LEMD3-related Buschke-Ollendorff syndrome with dermatological review and genetic counselling
